title: PostgreSQL With Raw SQL
summary: See what an ORM does and why this course skips it, then connect with node-postgres, run migrations, and write safe parameterized queries.
intro: Roombook's repository still keeps its bookings in a list, and the previous lesson designed the tables that will replace it. This lesson connects the two. It starts with a choice every project makes: most frameworks offer an ORM, a library that writes your SQL for you, and this course writes its own SQL with node-postgres, the `pg` package instead, for reasons part 1 explains. Then it opens a pool of database connections, creates the tables with migrations, reads rows without letting anyone inject SQL, writes rows, and turns the database's errors into API errors. By the end, the in-memory repository is gone, and the service never noticed.

steps.title: ORMs, and why this course writes SQL
steps.body:
Every Express project decides how its code talks to the database, and the choice shapes the rest of the code. The popular answer is an ORM. This course takes the other road and writes its SQL by hand. This part explains what an ORM does, what it costs, and why learning SQL first is the better start.

## What an ORM does

An **ORM**, an object-relational mapper, maps your classes to tables and your objects to rows. You describe a Booking class once, and the ORM writes the SQL. Saving a new object becomes an INSERT, changing a field and saving becomes an UPDATE, and a call like `prisma.booking.findMany({ where: { userId } })`, from Prisma, a popular ORM for Node, becomes a SELECT. Many ORMs also create the tables from your classes.

That's appealing. Simple endpoints need very little code, the types come for free, and you rarely write SQL at all.

## What it costs

- **You can't see the queries.** The SQL is made at run time, out of sight. A harmless-looking line can send a query that reads a whole table, and you find out when the endpoint is slow.
- **The N+1 problem.** You met N+1 with GraphQL's resolvers, and ORMs cause it the same way. Most load related rows lazily, the first time your code touches them. List 50 bookings and show each one's room name, and the ORM sends one query for the bookings, then one more for each booking's room: 51 queries where one JOIN would do. It's the most common reason ORM code is slow.
- **It's a second language.** Each ORM has its own way to write filters, joins, and groups, and whatever it can't express falls back to SQL. So you end up needing both.
- **It hides what the database can do.** The rules that keep Roombook correct, like refusing two bookings that overlap, are database features most ORMs can't describe. Teams on an ORM often skip them, and the rule moves into code that a second writer can get around.

## The spectrum

Database libraries fall along a line, from writing every query yourself to never seeing one:

```diagram raw-sql-spectrum
From writing every query yourself to never seeing one.
```

- A **driver** sends the SQL you write and hands back the rows. This course uses node-postgres, the `pg` package.
- A **query builder** builds SQL from function calls, which helps when a query changes shape at run time.
- **SQL-first** tools read SQL you write in files and give you typed functions that run it.
- An **ORM** maps classes to tables and writes the SQL itself.

| Step | Libraries for Node |
|---|---|
| Driver | `pg` (node-postgres), Postgres.js |
| Query builder | Kysely, Knex |
| SQL-first code generation | PgTyped |
| ORM | Prisma, Drizzle, TypeORM, Sequelize |

Drizzle and Kysely sit close to SQL and are fine choices later. This course skips them so the SQL stays in plain sight.

## Why this course writes SQL

You'll learn what the database really does, and every query Roombook sends sits in its repository, where you can read it, check it with EXPLAIN, and fix it. SQL also lasts. It's the same in every language and framework, so what you learn here carries over to your next project, while an ORM's API doesn't. And picking up an ORM once you know SQL is easy, because you can see through it. Going the other way is hard.

None of that makes ORMs wrong. Plenty of teams ship good software with one, especially apps that are mostly forms over tables. When you meet one, you'll know what it does underneath, and that's when it helps most.

steps.title: Connecting through a pool
Migrations in plain SQL
steps.body:
Your tables have to exist before the API can use them, and they'll change as Roombook grows: a new column, a new index, a new table. Every copy of the database, on your computer, on a teammate's, in the tests, and in production, needs exactly the same changes in the same order. Typing CREATE TABLE into psql on each one can't keep up. Migrations do.

## What a migration is

A **migration** is a file of SQL that changes the schema by one step, with a number in its name that sets its place in line. A **migration runner** keeps a table in the database that records which files have run. Each time, it applies the files that aren't in that table yet, in order, each inside a **transaction**, a group of statements that takes effect completely or not at all, and records them. So a fresh database gets every file, and one that's up to date gets none.

PostgreSQL can undo a CREATE TABLE or an ALTER TABLE that fails halfway, which many databases can't. So a migration that fails leaves nothing behind, and you can fix the file and run it again.

## The rules

- **Never edit a migration that has run anywhere but your own computer.** Other databases already applied the old version and won't run it again, so your change would reach some databases and not others. Fix it forward with a new migration.
- **One change per file, named for what it does**: `004_create_bookings.sql`, `005_add_bookings_no_overlap.sql`.
- **Keep data out of them, mostly.** Data to try things with, like Ada and the Turing room, goes in a separate seed script. A migration moves data only when the schema change needs it.
- **Make each change safe for the code that's already running.** While a new version rolls out, old copies of the API still run against the new schema. Adding a column is safe. Renaming one breaks the old code, so you add the new column, copy the data, switch the code over, and drop the old column in a later release.

## Roombook's first migrations

Roombook starts with four files, one per table, in the order the foreign keys need them: `migrations/001_create_buildings.sql`, `002_create_users.sql`, `003_create_rooms.sql`, and `004_create_bookings.sql`. Buildings come first, since rooms point at them, and bookings last. Here's `migrations/004_create_bookings.sql`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE bookings (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY (START WITH 1001) PRIMARY KEY,
  room_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES rooms (id),
  user_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id),
  starts_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  ends_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  attendees integer NOT NULL CHECK (attendees > 0),
  note text,
  status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'confirmed'
    CHECK (status IN ('confirmed', 'cancelled')),
  version integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  cancelled_at timestamptz,
  CHECK (ends_at > starts_at)
);

CREATE INDEX bookings_user_starts_idx ON bookings (user_id, starts_at);
CREATE INDEX bookings_room_starts_idx ON bookings (room_id, starts_at);
```

The other three files hold the CREATE TABLE statements from the data modeling lesson, with the CHECK rules, the foreign keys, and the unique index on `lower(email)` there from the start. The next lesson explains those rules, along with the one against overlapping bookings, which arrives in the fifth migration.

## The runner: a short script

Node has no standard migration tool, and Roombook needs very little, so a script of about forty lines does the job: `scripts/migrate.ts`, which the next example shows. It keeps its record in a table called `schema_migrations`, with one row per file that has run. It takes a lock first, `pg_advisory_lock`, a lock PostgreSQL holds under a number you choose, so that two servers starting at once don't both run the same file. Then it runs each new file in a transaction, adds its row, and commits, so a file either applies completely or not at all. A query with no parameters may hold several statements, which is how one call runs a whole file. It uses a single `pg.Client`, one connection with no pool, since a script that runs once needs nothing more.

Add it to `package.json` as `"migrate": "node --env-file-if-exists=.env scripts/migrate.ts"`, and run `npm run migrate` before you start the server, and as a step of every release, which the deploy lesson sets up.

examples.title: The migration script, and its first run
examples.prompt: `scripts/migrate.ts`, run with `npm run migrate` against an empty database.
examples.output:
> roombook@1.0.0 migrate
> node --env-file-if-exists=.env scripts/migrate.ts

applied 001_create_buildings.sql
applied 002_create_users.sql
applied 003_create_rooms.sql
applied 004_create_bookings.sql
examples.explanation: npm prints the script it's running, then each file the script applies. Running it again prints only npm's two lines, since every file is already in `schema_migrations`. If a file fails, its ROLLBACK undoes it completely, the error stops the script, and the files before it stay applied, so you fix the file and run the script again. `readdir` lists files in no promised order, so the `.sort()` puts them in name order, and that's why the names start with zero-padded numbers: `010` sorts after `009`, while `10` would sort before `9`. `import.meta.dirname` is the folder this script is in, so the script finds `migrations/` from anywhere you run it.

steps.title: Parameters, not string building

examples.title: An injection, and the same input as a parameter
examples.prompt: The first file shows the two queries the string-building code sends. The second runs the same lookup with a real parameter, in psql, using PREPARE, which names a statement with a placeholder, and EXECUTE, which runs it with a value.
examples.output:
id |        email         |  role
----+----------------------+--------
  1 | ada@roombook.example | member
(1 row)

 id |         email          |  role
----+------------------------+--------
  1 | ada@roombook.example   | member
  2 | grace@roombook.example | staff
  3 | alan@roombook.example  | admin
(3 rows)

PREPARE

 id |        email         |  role
----+----------------------+--------
  1 | ada@roombook.example | member
(1 row)

 id | email | role
----+-------+------
(0 rows)
examples.explanation: The first query finds Ada. The second is what the email `' OR '1'='1` turned the code's query into, and it returns all three users, Alan the admin included, without anyone knowing a password. The prepared version takes the same input as a value for `$1`. To write it in SQL, each quote inside the value is doubled, but PostgreSQL then sees one value: the text `' OR '1'='1`. No user has that email, so it finds none. That's exactly what the driver does for you on every query, with no doubling needed, since the values never mix with the text.

examples.title: What node-postgres hands back
examples.prompt: A quick script, `scripts/peek.ts`, that reads Ada's bookings straight from a pool with no type parser set, and prints the rows. Run it with `node --env-file=.env scripts/peek.ts`.
examples.explanation: Look at the ids. `id` and `room_id` are bigint columns, and they came back as strings, like `'1001'` and `'1'`, while `attendees`, an integer column, came back as the number 3. Without the type parser in `src/db/pool.ts`, an id would reach your JSON as `"1"`, and a check like `booking.userId === user.id` would quietly fail when one side is a string. `starts_at` is a real `Date`, printed in UTC with a `Z`. The second booking's note is NULL in the database, and `null` here. These rows come from the seed script, not from the bookings you made in memory, so this 1002 is Ada's Tuesday booking of Lovelace, with no note. The keys are the column names, snake_case, which is what `toBooking` maps to the domain's camelCase.

steps.title: Lists: filters, pages, and N+1

examples.title: Two pages of Ada's bookings
examples.prompt: With three more bookings seeded for her, 1004 to 1006, Ada has five, and a page holds two. Ask for three rows to learn whether there's a next page, then ask for the page after the last row shown.
examples.code:
-- Page 1: two bookings, plus one more to learn if a next page exists.
SELECT id, room_id, starts_at
FROM bookings
WHERE user_id = 1
ORDER BY starts_at, id
LIMIT 3;

-- Page 2: the rows after the last one shown, (2026-10-06 10:00, id 1002).
SELECT id, room_id, starts_at
FROM bookings
WHERE user_id = 1
  AND (starts_at, id) > ('2026-10-06 10:00Z', 1002)
ORDER BY starts_at, id
LIMIT 3;
examples.explanation: The first query returns three rows, one more than a page, so there's a next page. The API sends bookings 1001 and 1002, and builds the cursor from booking 1002: its start, 6 October at 10:00, and its id. The second query starts right after that pair and again gets three rows, so it sends 1004 and 1005, and there's a page after it too. Bookings 1005 and 1006 start at exactly the same moment, and only the id decides their order. Without it, the cut between two pages could fall between them and lose one. Booking 1003 never shows up, since it's Grace's.

steps.title: Writing rows and reading errors

examples.title: Writing, and getting the result back
examples.prompt: On the database as first seeded, with bookings 1001 to 1003, create a booking, change its attendees and clear its note in one UPDATE, then try to cancel booking 99.
examples.explanation: The INSERT gave the new booking the next id, 1004, and filled `status` and `version` from their defaults, and RETURNING sent them back with no second query. The UPDATE set two columns and bumped `version` to 2. Its note is NULL now, which psql prints as an empty space. The last UPDATE matched nothing, since there's no booking 99, so it reports `UPDATE 0` rather than an error, and the repository's count check is what turns that into a 404. `updated_at = now()` keeps the time of the last change, and the next lesson moves that job into the database.

examples.title: What a broken rule looks like in node-postgres
examples.prompt: A quick script, `scripts/fk.ts`, that tries to book room 99 and prints the error's fields.
examples.explanation: `code` is the SQLSTATE, `23503`, a foreign key violation. `constraint` names the exact rule, the foreign key PostgreSQL named for `bookings.room_id`. `detail` says which value broke it, and that's for your logs, not for the client, since a detail can include data the caller shouldn't see. `translate` reads only `code`, and answers with the domain's `room-not-found` problem, a 422. The `instanceof pg.DatabaseError` check first makes sure the error came from PostgreSQL, and not from a dropped connection or a bug in your own code.

recap:
- An ORM writes SQL for you and hides it, with N+1 queries as the classic cost, and this course writes SQL with node-postgres instead.
- A pool keeps a few connections open, each request borrows one, and the pool opens at startup and closes at shutdown.
- Migrations are numbered SQL files a runner applies once each, in order, in transactions, and a file that ran is never edited.
- Values always travel as parameters, never inside the SQL text, and names like sort columns come from an allowlist in the code.
- The repository maps rows to domain types and turns no row into not found, which the service answers with a 404.
- Optional filters and keyset pages build the WHERE from fixed pieces, and ANY or a JOIN replaces N+1 queries.
- RETURNING gives back what a write stored, the row count tells whether it found the row, and SQLSTATEs map to 409 or 422.
